name: Dana Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that writes courier-tracking software. I completed a two-year college diploma after years in office work, and I still need a senior to review tricky code. I have never used an AI tool; a printed scan trail lets me see why a customer got a wrong delivery notice. My partner drives a school bus, our son is grown, and we paid off our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot a parcel is delivered when the scan and the driver's sheet agree, not when a screen looks tidy. I write small fixes for a courier-tracking app, and I have never used an AI tool; I keep the printed scan trail beside my keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays mild, I expect our wages to keep coming. My developer pay is high even though I am still a junior after a two-year college diploma, my partner drives a school bus, our home is paid for, and we have ten months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep correcting duplicate-delivery bugs against the depot sheets. From next month we'd add 120 to our reserve while both wages hold, because I want to see actual retirement figures before deciding when to stop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Our home and savings give us room. A neighbour waiting for medicine still needs the right parcel at the right door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the double scan do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver scanned a medicine parcel at the same stop twice when the handheld froze. The app marked two deliveries, and I fixed the duplicate before the customer was told the second parcel had vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son cover retirement costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son lives nearby and fixes his own bicycles. He visits on Sundays, but his pay is for his household, not a line in our retirement plan.

say: I'd check **parcel scans** against the driver's delivery sheet.
I'd keep **customer notices** tied to real parcels, especially medicine.
think: I expect **two wages** to hold under modest AI change.
I have **ten months saved** and a paid-off home, but no checked pension figure.
do: Keep **fixing duplicate scans** against depot delivery sheets.
Save **120 extra monthly** while both wages hold and retirement figures remain unchecked.
feel: **Calm** about wages, careful with misdelivered medicine.
S0.quote: A neighbour waiting for medicine still needs the right parcel at the right door.
fieldNote: **Ten months saved** and high pay make current work and money secure alongside a paid-off home.
She favours **printed scan evidence** and has never used AI tools.

steps.text: Keep fixing duplicate parcel scans against depot delivery sheets
Save 120 extra monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write routine tracking fixes and answer customers before anyone checks the driver's sheet. A wrong delivery notice can make a family think medicine is missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink first, and I am not quick to learn a new system. Savings give us time, but at 58 I do not want a training promise in place of paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a list of duplicate medicine-parcel scans and take it to our weekly release review. My partner and I would postpone the planned kitchen refit until the firm gives a written junior-hours plan; I'd ask the depot manager what paid scanner-check posts exist, but change jobs only if a real opening and signed wage with bus-driver pay cover utilities, food and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours, though we can pay next month's bills. I want the customer to be able to call a person when the app says a parcel has arrived twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the duplicate-scan test show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper test should show one parcel, two scans and one delivery notice. I would not use an AI draft on live parcel records until someone proves it keeps that difference clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why defer the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen works; the cabinet doors are simply tired. We can leave the money in savings until we know whether both wages will continue.

say: I'd ask for **one-parcel evidence** before AI sends delivery notices.
I'd say **junior tracking fixes** may shrink before my retirement figures are clear.
think: I could lose **paid junior hours** despite our reserve.
I cannot call **a training promise** a replacement wage.
do: Keep **duplicate-scan list** for weekly release review.
Postpone **kitchen refit** until the firm gives a written junior-hours plan.
Change to **paid scanner checking** only with a real opening and signed household wages covering bills.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, able to defer a nonessential refit.
S1.quote: The kitchen works; the cabinet doors are simply tired.
fieldNote: **Routine tracking code** faces AI, placing her junior hours at risk despite strong savings.
She defers **a kitchen refit** and requires an actual paid depot opening before any job change.

steps.text: Keep logging duplicate medicine-parcel scans for weekly release review
Postpone kitchen refit until firm writes junior-hours plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues that thinking AGI by 2028 could write tracking code before delivery robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the depot not to remove the human route for disputing a missing medicine parcel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior post could go quickly. My partner’s bus wage covers basic utilities and food but not everything. Ten months saved gives a search period, not a verified retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask three nearby firms and the courier depot for real paid test or dispatch openings, hours and pay. If dismissed in the first year after 2028, I'd take a signed role only if its wage with my partner's covers utilities, food, travel and health costs; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using savings and ask the health insurer about coverage before a lapse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my own wage, even with a paid-off house. I would not ask our son to make up the difference; he has a household of his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show a new employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show an employer the anonymised medicine-parcel correction and its test. The test says one delivery after two scans; it does not show a customer's address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do bus hours affect the offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner needs to know whether new hours overlap the school-bus run. If they do and my partner loses paid runs, the combined wage still has to cover our bills.

say: I'd protect **human parcel disputes** if 2028 thinking AI replaces code.
I'd check **real paid openings** before promising a fallback.
think: I expect **my junior post** could disappear quickly.
I cannot replace **my wage** with an unchecked pension or my son's pay.
do: Check **three firms and depot** for actual paid test or dispatch openings, hours and pay.
After dismissal, take only **signed work** whose combined wages cover bills after any lost bus runs.
If none qualifies, seek **available paid work** using savings and check health coverage before it lapses.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of her wage despite ten months saved.
S2.quote: Ten months saved gives a search period, not a verified retirement income.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches tracking code before 2031 delivery robots.
A replacement needs **actual paid hours** and a wage floor after any effect on bus-driver shifts.

steps.text: Ask three nearby firms and depot about paid test or dispatch openings, hours and pay
Take signed post only if combined pay covers utilities, food, travel, health despite bus conflicts
If no post qualifies, use savings, check insurer before lapse and seek paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 is time to find out whether the depot still pays someone to test handheld scanners before a parcel leaves. Thinking AI reaches the tracking code then; delivery robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might move from junior coding into hands-on scanner checks, but I will not count a position the depot has not posted. I would rather keep earned wages than announce retirement at 63 without an income statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue logging the double-scan bug and ask the depot to let me observe one scanner-check shift only if my manager approves paid time. If a real post opens, the depot confirms I can do the lifting safely, and signed wages with my partner's cover utilities, food, travel and health costs after any bus-run conflict, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd move only on that written offer, otherwise keep paid development or seek other local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me see a real shift and a real pay slip. I do not need a shiny title; I need hours on a rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you handle the lifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scanner checker lifts a crate and tests whether one parcel produces one delivery mark. I have shoulder pain if I lift heavy boxes, so the depot would need to tell me the actual lifting limit before I accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your son support the move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son offered to help move boxes once, but that is different from paying our bills. I would discuss the shift and my shoulder with my partner, not make our son the fallback.

say: I'd ask for **real depot hours** and a safe lifting limit.
I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 delivery robots.
think: I cannot assume **scanner-check vacancy** or safe heavy lifting.
I still need **paid wages at 63** without a verified pension.
do: Keep **double-scan log** and observe depot shift only with manager-approved paid time.
Apply only if **real scanner vacancy**, safe lifting and signed household wages cover bills after bus-run conflicts.
After 2031, move only on **written qualifying offer**; otherwise keep paid development or seek paid local work if cut.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours and shoulder limits, able to inspect a shift.
S3.quote: I do not need a shiny title; I need hours on a rota.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow a paid shift observation but do not guarantee a depot opening or junior pay.
Her **shoulder limit** and bus-run conflicts materially affect whether the written wage is enough.

steps.text: Keep logging double scans during paid developer work

Take scanner vacancy only if lifting safe and signed pay covers bills after bus conflicts
Seek paid local work if developer wage ends without qualifying scanner offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 could take me to 68, but thinking AI would reach tracking code before delivery robots follow around 2039. I cannot tell a driver to retire from a date on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages, paid-off home and ten-month reserve feel secure. I have no retirement amount I have checked, and my partner's bus pay may also change by then, so I cannot promise we will stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the parcel tests and add 120 monthly to savings while both wages hold, then request our retirement statements and compare verified income with utilities, food, travel and health costs. In the first year after 2036 I'd leave paid work only if the verified combined income covers those bills; otherwise I'd keep an offered paid role or seek available local work within my shoulder limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant job picture, but calm enough about today's bills to do the arithmetic. I would not use my son's wage to make a retirement spreadsheet balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What example would you leave behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep one medicine-parcel double-scan example in the test file without the address. It reminds the next coder why a false 'delivered' message can matter on a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide on retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would check the statement amounts and start dates together. If the gap remains, we keep earning; if the figures cover our bills, then we can decide how much work to stop.

say: I'd compare **verified retirement income** with health and household costs.
I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches code before 2039 delivery robots.
think: I feel secure on **today's two wages** and paid-off home.
I cannot count **unknown pension** or my son's pay toward retirement.
do: Keep **parcel tests** and save 120 monthly while both wages hold.
Request **both retirement statements** and compare actual amounts and dates with household bills.
After 2036, stop paid work only if **verified income covers bills**; otherwise seek available work within shoulder limits.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant earnings while present finances are sound.
S4.quote: I would not use my son's wage to make a retirement spreadsheet balance.
fieldNote: **Present wages and reserve** support relative ease without assuming future pension income.
She makes retirement depend on **verified bills and income**, with any continued work within her shoulder limit.

steps.text: Keep correcting parcel tests while current developer wage lasts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the junior coding wage could go before a real paid depot or testing post appears. Written notice, an honest lifting limit and signed hours would help us judge offers without calling savings a pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask about my shoulder. A depot can call a job 'scanner testing,' but if it means lifting heavy crates all day I cannot safely take it, whatever the title says.

headlineQuote: A depot can call a job 'scanner testing,' but if it means lifting heavy crates all day I cannot safely take it, whatever the title says.
portrait: Dana, **58**, is a junior courier-tracking developer with a two-year diploma who checks code against printed parcel scans.
Her **higher pay**, partner's bus wage, paid-off home, ten-month reserve and local employers make current money secure.
She has **never used AI** and focuses on duplicate medicine-parcel scans rather than new tool claims.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a paid depot fallback requires a posted vacancy, safe lifting, compatible bus hours and signed wages.
She will **verify retirement income** before leaving work and will not budget her grown son's earnings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior wage before a qualifying paid local vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, honest lifting limits and signed hours would let her judge real offers.
